newsitem.title: TURKEY: FEATURE-Turkey seeks new textile markets.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Turkey seeks new textile markets.

text.p: Tulin Aygunes

Turkey's textile and ready-to-wear industries expect strong growth in 1997, boosted by strong investment, new markets and a switch to selling own-brand goods and away from sub-contracted output for foreign companies.

"Despite last year's difficulties, we expect a rise of around 25-30 percent in exports with the help of investments accumulated in recent years, high technology and human resources," Mehment Yasar Akcay, general manager of the leading textile exporter Ege Giyim Sanayicileri (EGS) Dis Ticaret A.S, told Reuters.

Last year was disappointing because of the handicap of an overvalued Turkish lira, difficulties in adjusting to a customs union with Europe, a slump in European markets and intense competition, industry leaders said.

Turkish textile exports, led by clothing items, totalled $8.79 billion in 1996, down from $9 billion the previous year, according to the unofficial but reliable Turkish Exporters Union (TIM) data. It put Turkey's total exports at $23.69 billion in 1996 up from $22.4 billion in 1995.
TIM said textile and readywear exports were $1.67 billion in the first two months of 1997, up 24 percent from $1.35 billion in the same 1996 period.
NEW MARKETS BUOY PRODUCTION

Factors underlying this year's growth include diversification of products with new investments, new markets, better adaption to customs union and sales of own brands instead of production for other labels, sector officials say.
Turkish exporters encountered problems in the EU countries after the customs union took effect in January 1996 because local regulations were not brought into line with the EU system.
Officials said Turkey began this year to take advantage of the union, which eliminated customs taxes, after adapting most of its foreign trade regulations to the EU.
A slowdown in Europe, mainly in Germany, Turkey's biggest trade partner, undermined textile and readywear exports in 1996.
Turkey's market share in Europe also fell because of stiff competition from the Far East.

"Turkey should maintain its potential in the European Union and the United States but should also seek new markets and fight against the strong competition abroad,," Uslu Holding, a leading towel and bathrobe exporter to the United States, said in a statement.
EGS's Akcay said Turkey eyed northern America, Russia and Turkic republics as new potential markets.
VALUE FROM OWN BRANDS
The export to Europe from the Far East of cheaper but lower-quality readywear put pressure on Turkish exports. But officials said this could be overcome by creating new brands.

A report by Istanbul Textile and Readywear Exporters' Union said Turkey should market its own brand products rather than subcontracting for foreign companies because of fierce competition both in and outside the country.
Officials say improved technology in recent years would help Turkey to create brands which would also boost the value contributed to the economy.

"We were mainly the subcontractor of Europe, but we should create our own brands and target fashion centres like France and Italy as competitors. If we can sell our own brands, we will also earn more," Akcay said.

Turkey mostly exports home textiles (curtains, fabrics, bed sheets), readywear (bathrobes, towels, t-shirts, jeans, cotton wear) to Europe and the United States, where such products are sold under different local and international brands.
ECONOMIC AND POLITICAL STABILITY
Officials point out that Turkey's economic and political stability and state incentives for investments will also support the sector's growth in the future.
Exporters blamed an overvalued Turkish lira in 1996, as well as higher energy and raw material costs, for the decline in textile and readywear exports.
The dollar gained only 80.7 percent and the mark 66.3 percent against the lira in 1996 compared with wholesale inflation of 85 percent.

"Turkey imposes a policy of foreign currency stability in line with the inflation. But a realistic foreign currency policy fuels exports, so the foreign currencies should not be undervalued," Uslu Holding said in its statement.
